# Reference palette

This is the **reference instance** of the data-viz method: every parameter the
method needs, filled in with a validated default palette. The rest of the skill
is system-agnostic - **to target your brand, substitute this file's values** and
re-run the validator. Nothing else changes.

## How to use these values

Everything below is plain hex. In an HTML chart, **define the slots you use as
CSS custom properties in a local `<style>` block** at the top of the file, then
reference them by role throughout - so the light/dark values swap in one place,
and the chart body is written against roles rather than raw hex:

```css
.viz-root {
  color-scheme: light;
  --surface-1:      #fcfcfb;   /* chart surface */
  --text-primary:   #0b0b0b;
  --text-secondary: #52514e;
  --series-1:       #2a78d6;   /* categorical slot 1 */
  /* ...only the roles this chart uses */
}
@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark) {
  :root:where(:not([data-theme="light"])) .viz-root {
    color-scheme: dark;
    --surface-1:      #1a1a19;
    --text-primary:   #ffffff;
    --text-secondary: #c3c2b7;
    --series-1:       #3987e5;
  }
}
:root[data-theme="dark"] .viz-root {
  color-scheme: dark;
  --surface-1:      #1a1a19;
  --text-primary:   #ffffff;
  --text-secondary: #c3c2b7;
  --series-1:       #3987e5;
}
```

Declare the dark values under both scopes as above - the media query covers
the OS setting; the `data-theme` scope covers the viewer's theme toggle,
which must win both ways (the `:not(...)` guard lets a light stamp beat
OS-dark; `:where()` keeps the media block below the toggle scope).

## Categorical palette

Both modes are selected. The dark column is the same eight hues stepped for the
dark surface, not a separate palette:

| Slot | Hue | Light | Dark |
|------|-----|-------|------|
| 1 | blue | `#2a78d6` | `#3987e5` |
| 2 | orange | `#eb6834` | `#d95926` |
| 3 | aqua | `#1baf7a` | `#199e70` |
| 4 | yellow | `#eda100` | `#c98500` |
| 5 | magenta | `#e87ba4` | `#d55181` |
| 6 | green | `#008300` | `#008300` |
| 7 | violet | `#4a3aa7` | `#9085e9` |
| 8 | red | `#e34948` | `#e66767` |

This order passes every hard gate in both modes on the default *adjacent*
pairlist (stacks, bars, lines): worst adjacent CVD Delta E 9.1 light / 8.4 dark
(OKLab ×100, >=8 target), worst adjacent normal-vision Delta E 19.6 light / 19.3
dark (>=15 floor). Under `--pairs all` (scatter, bubble, choropleth, small
multiples) the full eight cannot clear the floors - with all 28 pairs in
play no ordering can (the pairlist no longer depends on order), and
re-stepping is off the table by the documented-palette rule - so those
chart forms carry a series cap: **the first three slots validate all-pairs
in both modes** (worst pair CVD Delta E 9.2 light / 9.4 dark, normal-vision 24.0
light / 20.9 dark - clear of the CVD warn band). Past three, fold to "Other" or
facet: the fourth slot puts yellow and orange on screen
together, and that pair fails the all-pairs floors (normal-vision 13.7
light; CVD 4.8 dark). Three light-mode slots (magenta, yellow, aqua)
sit below 3:1 contrast on the light surface: the **relief rule** applies (ship
visible direct labels or the table view). The dark steps were chosen for the
dark band (OKLCH L ~ 0.48-0.67, >= 3:1 on the dark surface) and validated as a
set. (Ordering history: adopted July 2026 for its more harmonious opening -
the same eight hues and steps as its predecessor, re-ordered, zero hex
changes. The predecessor validated its first FOUR slots all-pairs, with its
dark run in the 6-8 CVD warn band, so secondary encoding was required there;
this order deliberately trades that fourth slot - yellow now sits beside orange -
for better-looking leading colors. Revisit the trade if yellow<->orange
confusion shows up in real charts with four or more series; undoing it is a
pure re-order.) When you swap in your own ramps, hold your palette to the full
gate.

The slot **ordering** is the CVD-safety mechanism, not cosmetic - candidate
orderings were enumerated and only those clearing every adjacent gate in both
modes kept (see `color-formula.md` § Themes); this default is one of the
passing orders, picked among them for its opening colors. When you swap in
your brand's hues, do the same: run the validator on candidate orderings and
choose only among the passing ones.

## Sequential hue

Default single hue: **blue**, light->dark. When two sequential contexts appear at
once, the second takes the next categorical slot's hue (orange), each as its own
one-hue ramp.

| step | hex | step | hex | step | hex | step | hex |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 100 | `#cde2fb` | 250 | `#86b6ef` | 400 | `#3987e5` | 550 | `#1c5cab` |
| 150 | `#b7d3f6` | 300 | `#6da7ec` | 450 | `#2a78d6` | 600 | `#184f95` |
| 200 | `#9ec5f4` | 350 | `#5598e7` | 500 | `#256abf` | 650 | `#104281` |
| | | | | | | 700 | `#0d366b` |

The full 100->700 range is for **sequential** encoding (continuous magnitude -
heatmaps, choropleths) where the lightest step means "near zero" and is allowed
to recede toward the surface. For an **ordinal** ramp (discrete ordered marks -
funnel stages, tiers - validated with `--ordinal`), the step nearest the surface
must still clear 2:1: on light, start no lighter than **step 250** (`#86b6ef`,
2.06:1); on dark, go no darker than **step 600** (`#184f95`, 2.15:1).

## Diverging pair

**blue <-> red** - warm/cool poles that read as opposite. Neutral midpoint is gray
(light `#f0efec`, dark `#383835`). Equal step count per arm. (blue<->aqua was
rejected - both cool, the midpoint doesn't read as "nothing".)

## Status palette (fixed - never themed)

| role | hex | light-surface contrast | dark-surface contrast |
|---|---|---|---|
| good | `#0ca30c` | 3.27 | 5.19 |
| warning | `#fab219` | 1.79 | 9.49 |
| serious | `#ec835a` | 2.57 | 6.60 |
| critical | `#d03b3b` | 4.68 | 3.62 |

Dark: same four steps - all clear 3:1 on the dark surface (`#1a1a19`) and remain
distinct from the dark categorical slots. On the light surface, warning and
serious are sub-3:1 by design; the **icon + label** pairing is the mitigation, so
a status color never carries meaning alone. These steps are deliberately distinct
from the categorical slots so a status color never impersonates a series -
distinct enough that nothing collides at a glance, not enough for hue to
carry the distinction unaided: measured by the series floor's own bar
(unsimulated Delta E >= 15), around nine categorical-vs-status pairs per mode sit
below 15 - in light mode red vs critical and yellow vs warning both measure
4.8, slot-2 orange sits 5.8 from status-serious, and the light success text
green `#006300` sits 10.1 from the series green; green vs status-good (9.7)
holds in both modes, since both hexes are mode-invariant. The rule is general: any series color beside a
same-hue-family status or delta cue leans on the icon + label pairing and on
placement; never on hue alone.

## Texture fill (the accessibility channel)

One hand-drawn **"Lines"** fill, used at **45° and its 135° mirror only**. Inked
tone-on-tone (a darker step of the fill's own ramp). On value scales it is
*ordered* (rotation steps with magnitude; arm angle carries the diverging sign).

# Interaction - tooltips & filters

An HTML chart is interactive by default - the hover layer is part of the deliverable,
not an upgrade. Omitting it is the exception (a bare stat tile), never the default.
Design it with the same care as the static render.

## Tooltips & hover

Tooltips **enhance, they never gate**: every value a tooltip shows is also reachable
without it, through direct labels or the table view. Same details on keyboard focus
as on hover.

- **The crosshair finds the X.** A vertical hairline tracks the pointer and snaps to
  the nearest data position. Readers aim at a date, never at a 2px line.
- **On bars and cells, the mark is the hit target.** No crosshair - each bar, segment,
  dot, or heat-cell carries its own `pointermove`/`focus` tooltip showing category and
  value, and the hovered mark lifts (slight lighten or outline) so the reader sees it respond.
- **One tooltip, every series.** The readout lists every series at that X - the
  pointer never has to land on a line or a fill to get a value.
- **Labels are untrusted data - use `textContent`.** Series and category names
  often come from CSV headers, tool output, or API responses. Insert them into
  tooltip/legend/table DOM with `textContent` or `createTextNode`, never via
  `innerHTML` string concatenation.
- **Values lead, labels follow.** In the tooltip the value is the Strong,
  high-contrast element and the series name is secondary - the legend's hierarchy
  inverted, because here the reader has the series and wants the number.
- **Line keys, not boxes.** Tooltip rows key their series with a short stroke of the
  series color; at tooltip density a filled box is data-weight ink doing a label's
  job. (Legends still mirror the mark: rect for bars/areas, line for lines.)
- **The hit target is bigger than the mark.** A mark's hover/focus area includes its
  2px surface gap and then some - never only the painted pixels. An 8px scatter dot is a
  pinpoint nobody hits reliably; give each point a transparent hit area of at least
  **24px**, or - for dense scatter - a nearest-point / Voronoi layer so the pointer only
  has to be *closest*, not dead-center. (The crosshair already does this for the X on
  line and bar charts; scatter and bubble need the per-point version.)
- **A value pushed off its mark lives in the tooltip.** When a label won't fit inside a
  small bar (see `marks-and-anatomy.md`), that bar's hit area carries the value on hover
  and focus - the tooltip is its overflow home, and the table view keeps it reachable
  without hovering at all.

## Filters & time ranges

Every monitoring dashboard needs the same controls. These are **standard UI, not
chart marks** - build them with ordinary HTML form controls styled to match the
chart chrome. Dataviz only adds composition rules:

- **One row, above the charts.** Filters sit in a single left-aligned row above the
  content they scope - never inside a chart card, never per-chart. If one chart needs
  its own range, it's a different dashboard.
- **Date range first.** It's the filter every reader reaches for; presets (today,
  last 7 / 30 / 90 days) before a custom range.
- **Filters scope everything below them.** Every chart, stat, and table re-renders
  against the same slice, so the numbers always agree.
- **Refetch keeps the frame.** While data reloads, charts hold their previous render
  at reduced opacity - no skeleton, no layout jump, no flash.

A good date picker lists presets as rows (nobody fights a calendar grid for "last 30
days"), marks selection with a 16px bold check, keeps hover a ghost wash so it never
competes with selection, and tucks the custom range behind a hairline in the footer.
(See `palette.md` for the reference spec.)

input.content:
# DataTraceMind

An agentic data-reliability engineer. It detects when a data pipeline is
producing wrong numbers, investigates the cause with evidence from the source
database, the pipeline, the analytics target, and the approved business
rules, proposes a minimal repair, proves that repair in staging, and applies
it only after a human approves that exact change.

The failure it is built around is the silent one: the ETL job reports
`SUCCESS` while the revenue it loaded is wrong.

Built for neatHack (10–12 October 2026). The build log and submission
evidence are in [hackathon.md](hackathon.md).

## What happens in one incident

1. A simulator writes orders, payments, and refunds to PostgreSQL (`oltp`).
2. A Python ETL loads the analytics schema, driven by a versioned
   transformation file.
3. The scenario lab injects one known fault.
4. Deterministic quality checks fail and the monitor opens an incident. No
   model decides that something is wrong.
5. A supervisor runs the agent roles: a source-data investigator and a
   pipeline investigator in parallel, a contract lookup, a root-cause analyst,
   and a repair agent. Each model-backed role is one Codex turn with its own
   tool allow-list and output schema.
6. The repair is run in a staging schema against regression fixtures and every
   quality check.
7. A person reviews the evidence, diff, and staging result, then approves or
   rejects. Approval is bound to the patch hash.
8. On approval the patch is applied, the pipeline reruns, and the incident
   resolves only if every check passes. Otherwise it rolls back.

## Run it

Requirements: Docker, Python 3.13, Node.js 22 or newer, and the
[Codex CLI](https://developers.openai.com/codex/cli) signed in (`codex login`)
or `CODEX_API_KEY` set. Without model credentials everything except
"Investigate" still works; that button is refused with a message saying why.

```sh
cp .env.example .env                  # add NEATLOGS_API_KEY to trace agent runs
docker compose up -d postgres
python3.13 -m venv .venv && .venv/bin/pip install -r requirements.txt
(cd frontend && npm install && npm run build)
.venv/bin/uvicorn datatracemind.api.app:app --port 8000
```

Open <http://127.0.0.1:8000>. The first start seeds a deterministic baseline.

Demo path: **Scenario lab → Inject fault (DS-01) → Investigate → review the
repair → Approve and apply**. **Reset demo** returns to the clean baseline.
An investigation takes about a minute and four Codex turns.

For frontend development, `npm run dev` in `frontend/` serves the dashboard on
port 5173 and proxies `/api` to port 8000.

## Scenarios

| ID | Fault | What the checks see |
|---|---|---|
| DS-01 | A transformation change stops subtracting completed refunds | ETL green; net revenue overstated by exactly the succeeded refunds |
| DS-02 | A source migration renames `orders.total_amount` | ETL fails; analytics goes stale |
| DS-03 | The order fact is built with an inner join to payments | ETL green; orders with no payment are missing |

Each scenario carries an answer key (`ground_truth`) that only the evaluator
reads. Nothing an agent can call, and no prompt, contains it.

## Safety model

- **Agents only read.** The investigation tools connect with a PostgreSQL role
  that can `SELECT` from the source, the analytics target, and the
  transformation history, and nothing else. No tool accepts SQL; queries are
  templates with typed parameters.
- **Codex has no shell.** Each turn runs with the shell and web search
  disabled and a read-only sandbox, so the MCP tools are its only reach.
- **Evidence comes from tool results.** The adapter reads the tool calls from
  Codex's event stream and fails a turn unless the role's required calls
  succeeded. The model's description of a result is never stored as evidence.
- **A repair is data, not code.** It is a new version of one allowlisted file,
  `etl/transforms/order_revenue.yaml`, and is accepted only if it parses
  against a strict schema and changes a handful of lines.
- **Deterministic checks decide.** Staging validation, approval checks, and
  post-fix verification are code. A model's statement that something passed
  proves nothing.
- **Approval is bound to the patch.** The executor re-reads the proposal, the
  approval, and the validation result and refuses unless all three name the
  same hash and the patch still applies to the deployed version.
- **Prompts are fixed templates.** No text typed into the web application
  reaches a prompt. Mutating routes can require a demo access code, and
  investigations are capped per hour and per day.
- **Unclear business rules go to a human.** A missing contract, or a rule the
  analyst cannot find, escalates the incident instead of being assumed.

## Tests and evaluation

```sh
.venv/bin/python -m pytest                           # 99 tests, about a minute
.venv/bin/python -m datatracemind.evaluation DS-01   # one real run, scored
```

The tests use a separate `datatracemind_test` database and spend no model
usage: the workflow is driven by a scripted stand-in provider whose tool calls
are real. They cover the blocked paths as well as the happy one: applying
without approval, a changed patch after approval, a patch that failed
validation, rejection, and a failed post-fix verification.

The evaluator resets the demo, injects a scenario, runs a real investigation,
and scores it against the answer key. Results are written to
`evaluation/results/`.

## Layout

```
contracts/        approved business definitions (revenue, orders, source schema)
etl/              pipeline, transformation, quality checks, run log
simulator/        seeded transaction generator
infra/postgres/   schema for source, analytics target, and application state
datatracemind/
  api/            FastAPI routes
  monitoring/     detection and dashboard read models
  scenarios/      fault scenarios and their answer keys
  tools/          read-only investigation tools and the MCP server
  llm/            provider contract and the Codex adapter
  agents/         role prompts and the role runner
  orchestration/  supervisor state machine and routing
  repair/         proposals, staging validation, approval, executor
  observability/  neatlogs tracing
  evaluation.py   scenario evaluator
frontend/         React dashboard
tests/
```

## Hackathon tools

- **neatlogs** traces every investigation: one trace per run, a span per role,
  per Codex turn (with token usage and estimated cost), and per tool call.
  Approval, apply, and verification are traced as guardrail spans in the same
  session.
- **Entire** captures the coding-agent sessions behind each commit.
- **cfo.ai** holds the business plan; the measured cost per investigation
  feeds it.

## Deviations from the plan

- The simulator is Python, not Spring Boot. The `oltp` schema is its only
  interface to the pipeline, so another producer can replace it.
- The analytics target is a PostgreSQL schema, the plan's documented fallback
  to ClickHouse.
- The ETL worker runs as a thread inside the API process rather than as its
  own service.
- Contract lookup runs before the two investigators rather than beside them,
  so a missing definition escalates before any model usage is spent.
- Two database credentials exist (application and read-only), not a third
  repair-only one. The executor's single write is deploying a new version of
  the transformation file.

## Known limitations

- Only DS-01 has been run end to end with the real model so far. DS-02 and
  DS-03 pass end to end with the scripted provider.
- Cost figures are estimates at API list prices; the model runs on a
  flat-rate ChatGPT plan.
- There is no container image for the API yet, and the stack has not been
  deployed.

"""Export measured cost per investigation as CSV, for the cfo.ai business plan.

    python -m datatracemind.cost_export > business-plan/investigation_costs.csv

One row per evaluated run, read from evaluation/results/. Token counts are
measured. `est_cost_usd` is an estimate at API list prices: the model runs on
a flat-rate plan, so nothing was charged per run. Only summaries are written;
no source rows, prompts, or secrets.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import csv
import json
import sys

from datatracemind.evaluation import RESULTS_DIR

COLUMNS = (
    "run_date", "incident_id", "scenario_id", "workflow_version", "model", "outcome", "role_turns",
    "tool_calls", "input_tokens", "cached_input_tokens", "output_tokens", "est_cost_usd", "duration_s",
)  # fmt: skip


def rows() -> list[dict]:
    exported = []
    for path in sorted(RESULTS_DIR.glob("*.json")):
        result = json.loads(path.read_text())
        run = result["run"]
        exported.append(
            {
                "run_date": result["evaluated_at"][:10],
                "incident_id": result["incident_id"],
                "scenario_id": result["scenario_id"],
                "workflow_version": result["workflow_version"],
                "model": result["model"],
                "outcome": result["outcome"],
                **{name: run[name] for name in COLUMNS if name in run and name not in ("incident_id",)},
            }
        )
    return exported


def main() -> None:
    writer = csv.DictWriter(sys.stdout, fieldnames=COLUMNS, extrasaction="ignore")
    writer.writeheader()
    writer.writerows(rows())


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

# neatHack build log — DataTraceMind

Running log of what was built, what was actually tested, what failed, and
where the evidence is. Newest session first. Times are IST.

## Evidence checklist

| Required evidence | Status | Where |
|---|---|---|
| Code: public repo, commits dated in the hackathon | Commits made from 13:10 on 10 Oct on branch `build/ds01-vertical-slice`; **not pushed yet** | `git log` |
| neatlogs: traces from the project | One full DS-01 investigation exported; **not yet opened in the dashboard by a person** | Trace ID `d931c993a7f032e18558ce61ea460904` |
| Entire: checkpoint link and ID | Seven commits each carry an `Entire-Checkpoint` trailer; links work after the branch is pushed | Table under Session 1 |
| The agent improved: before/after pair | Baseline ("before") run recorded; **"after" run not done yet** | `evaluation/results/20261010-133338-DS-01-v1.json` |
| Recovery from failure | Covered by tests with a scripted provider; **no traced real run yet** | `tests/test_workflow.py` |
| cfo.ai business plan | Not started. Measured cost per investigation is exported and ready to upload | `business-plan/investigation_costs.csv` |
| Building in public: `#neatHack` posts | None yet | – |
| Demo video | Not recorded | – |

## Session 1 — 10 October 2026, 12:50–14:10

Coding agent: Claude Code (Opus 5.5), inside an Entire-enabled session.

### What was built

Phases 1 to 4 of the product brief, and a first pass at the Phase 5 dashboard.

- **Data path.** PostgreSQL with an `oltp` source schema and an `analytics`
  target schema; a seeded Python simulator; an ETL that extracts from one
  repeatable-read snapshot, transforms through a versioned transformation
  file, and loads idempotently; twelve deterministic quality checks derived
  from the contracts.
- **Scenario lab and detection.** DS-01 (refund logic), DS-02 (schema drift),
  DS-03 (join loss). The monitor opens one incident per unresolved problem
  with a severity from fixed thresholds.
- **Agent workflow.** Twelve read-only investigation tools behind an MCP
  server; a Codex adapter that fails a turn unless its required tool calls
  succeeded; a supervisor state machine with bounded retries and escalation.
- **Repair lifecycle.** Hashed, immutable proposals; staging validation;
  approval bound to the patch hash; a guarded executor; post-fix verification
  with automatic rollback.
- **Dashboard.** Overview, scenario lab, incident page with evidence and
  repair review, audit log.
- **Evaluator.** `python -m datatracemind.evaluation DS-01` scores a real run
  against the scenario's answer key.

### What was tested

- `pytest`: **99 passed** in 65 s. Uses a separate test database and a
  scripted stand-in provider, so it spends no model usage. Covers DS-01,
  DS-02, and DS-03 end to end, and the blocked paths: apply without approval,
  a patch changed after approval, a patch that failed validation, rejection,
  an agent role name used as approver, and a failed post-fix verification.
- **One real DS-01 investigation** with Codex (`gpt-6-sol`, medium effort),
  workflow version `v1`, from a clean reset:

  | Measure | Value |
  |---|---|
  | Outcome | `awaiting_approval` (stopped at the human decision, as designed) |
  | Root-cause category | `refund_logic` — correct |
  | Repair | `refund_statuses: [COMPLETED]` → `[SUCCEEDED]`, one line — correct |
  | Staging validation | passed: 10 of 10 regression cases, 12 of 12 quality checks |
  | Apply before approval | refused |
  | Duration | 70.1 s (detected → diagnosed: 46.9 s) |
  | Role turns / tool calls | 4 / 11, none failed, no retries |
  | Tokens | 219,595 input (112,384 cached), 3,874 output |
  | Estimated cost | $0.28 at API list prices (the plan is flat-rate; nothing was charged) |

- **Dashboard** opened in Chrome against that incident: overview, chart
  tooltip, incident page, repair review, and audit log render with no console
  errors. Checked in dark mode only.

### Not tested

- The approval → apply → verify path with a **real model's** patch. The
  incident above was left at `awaiting_approval`: approving is a human
  decision. The same path passes in tests with scripted patches.
- DS-02 and DS-03 with the real model.
- The neatlogs trace in the dashboard. The exporter reported no failures, but
  reading a trace back needs `neatlogs auth login --device`, a human step.
  Nesting was checked locally without export: role spans on worker threads
  share the run's trace ID.
- Light mode, and narrow screens.
- Running in a container or on Linux.

### What failed or surprised, and what was done

- The first schema-drift test passed when it should have failed: an
  incremental run with no changed rows never queried the renamed column.
  The extraction queries now run on every pass.
- `mcp` 2.x hides the text of any exception except its own `ToolError`. Tool
  refusals ("column does not exist; columns are …") are now raised as that
  type so the model can correct its call; other exception text stays hidden.
- Codex reports a tool-level error with `error: null` and the message in the
  result text, not in `error.message` as the provider notes assumed. The
  adapter now reads both.
- `mcp_servers.dtm.env_vars` forwards named environment variables to the tool
  server (verified: the server used the database named in the forwarded
  variable). This avoids putting a connection string on the command line.

### Weaknesses seen in the baseline run (candidates for the before/after change)

1. The pipeline investigator read `etl/pipeline.py` and the interpreter source
   in addition to the transformation file: 6 tool calls and 86,868 input
   tokens, the most expensive turn, for an incident the transformation file
   and its history already explain.
2. The analyst cited ten of twelve evidence items as support instead of the
   few that carry the argument, and widened the implicated component to
   include `etl/pipeline.py`.
3. The analyst reported 100% confidence.

### Commits and Entire checkpoints

Link format once pushed:
`https://entire.io/gh/siddarth-ba-72/DataTraceMind/commit/<commit>`

| Commit | Subject | Checkpoint ID |
|---|---|---|
| `1586fce5` | Track Entire configuration | `01M4JC31XBG5KVAZJ40KW03ZAZ` |
| `c6a7714e` | Add source schema, simulator, ETL, and quality checks | `01M4JC34TY7PVQZMZ4RSR6R930` |
| `eb080a60` | Add scenario lab, detection, incident store, and API | `01M4JC373DVME39XHCGK4Q5N9M` |
| `3b17cf74` | Add read-only investigation tools, MCP tool server, and Codex adapter | `01M4JD770W9AZS179A1XKV4WCY` |
| `aa18140d` | Add supervisor workflow and the repair lifecycle | `01M4JD79M2NQEF9Y9MYB1GYCWX` |
| `db2e9502` | Add scenario evaluator and record the first real DS-01 run | `01M4JDHC7V0EP4R9GJA1G5FA37` |

### Decisions made this session

- Analytics target: a PostgreSQL schema (the brief's fallback to ClickHouse).
- Simulator: Python, behind the same `oltp` schema a Spring Boot one would use.
- The transformation is a declarative, versioned file. A repair is a
  schema-checked change to that file, never generated code or SQL.
- Investigations start from a button by default (`DTM_AUTO_INVESTIGATE=1`
  starts them on detection), to conserve the shared Codex allowance.

### Next

1. Human: push the branch; open the trace in neatlogs; approve INC-0001 in the
   dashboard to exercise apply and verify with a real patch.
2. Change one thing from the weaknesses above, bump the workflow version to
   `v2`, rerun DS-01, and record the before/after numbers.
3. Capture a traced recovery run.
4. Run DS-02 and DS-03 with the real model.
5. Container image and deployment; cfo.ai plan; demo video.

import pathlib, re
p = pathlib.Path("etl/pipeline.py")
s = p.read_text()
old = '''# Serialises everything that reads or rewrites pipeline state in this process:
# scheduled runs, staging validation, fault injection, repair, and reset.
PIPELINE_LOCK = threading.RLock()
'''
new = '''_THREAD_LOCK = threading.RLock()
_ADVISORY_LOCK_KEY = 0x44544D01
_lock_holder: ExitStack | None = None
_lock_depth = 0


@contextmanager
def pipeline_lock() -> Iterator[None]:
    """Serialise everything that reads or rewrites pipeline state.

    Scheduled runs, staging validation, fault injection, repair, and reset all
    take it. It is re-entrant, and it holds across processes as well as
    threads (a PostgreSQL advisory lock on its own connection), so the API's
    worker and a script such as the evaluator can share one database.
    """
    global _lock_holder, _lock_depth
    with _THREAD_LOCK:
        if _lock_depth == 0:
            holder = ExitStack()
            conn = holder.enter_context(connect(autocommit=True))
            conn.execute("SELECT pg_advisory_lock(%s)", (_ADVISORY_LOCK_KEY,))
            _lock_holder = holder
        _lock_depth += 1
        try:
            yield
        finally:
            _lock_depth -= 1
            if _lock_depth == 0 and _lock_holder is not None:
                # Closing the session releases the advisory lock.
                _lock_holder.close()
                _lock_holder = None
'''
assert s.count(old) == 1
s = s.replace(old, new)
s = s.replace("import time\nfrom dataclasses import dataclass, field\n", "import time\nfrom collections.abc import Iterator\nfrom contextlib import ExitStack, contextmanager\nfrom dataclasses import dataclass, field\n")
assert s.count("    with PIPELINE_LOCK:\n") == 1
s = s.replace("    with PIPELINE_LOCK:\n", "    with pipeline_lock():\n")
p.write_text(s)

content.text:
Written for: the README is for people opening the repository (judges, teammates); `hackathon.md` is for the neatHack judges and your team.

Phases 1–4 of the brief are built, plus a first-pass dashboard, and DS-01 runs end to end with the real model up to the human approval step. Everything is on branch `build/ds01-vertical-slice` (11 commits, each with an Entire checkpoint), not pushed.

## What works
- **Data path, detection and scenario lab:** DS-01 (refund logic), DS-02 (schema drift) and DS-03 (join loss) each open one incident from deterministic checks.
- **Agent workflow:** two real DS-01 investigations with Codex found the correct root cause, proposed the one-line fix (`refund_statuses: [COMPLETED]` → `[SUCCEEDED]`), passed staging validation and stopped at approval. Each took 70–75 s and four Codex turns, about $0.27 at API list prices.
- **Safety rules:** applying without approval, a patch changed after approval, a patch that failed validation, and an agent name used as approver are all refused.
- **Tests:** 100 pass. They use a separate test database and a scripted stand-in for the model, so they spend no Codex usage.
- **Dashboard:** overview, scenario lab, incident page with repair review, and audit log render without console errors (checked in dark mode only).

## What is not verified
- **Apply and verify with a real model's patch.** I left INC-0001 at "awaiting approval" because approving is your decision. The same path passes in tests with scripted patches.
- **DS-02 and DS-03 with the real model.** They pass end to end only with the scripted stand-in.
- **The traces in the neatlogs dashboard.** The exporter reported no failures, but reading a trace back needs the neatlogs CLI login, which is a human step. Trace IDs are in [hackathon.md](hackathon.md).
- **The before/after improvement.** I made one prompt change (workflow v2) and reran DS-01. Correctness held, but tool calls only went 11 → 10, estimated cost fell under 5%, and total tokens and duration rose. That is within run-to-run noise, so it should not be presented as an improvement; the log lists two better-targeted changes.

## Decisions I made that you may want to reverse
- The simulator is Python, not Spring Boot; the brief allows a lightweight equivalent, and the source schema is its only interface.
- Analytics is a PostgreSQL schema, the brief's fallback to ClickHouse.
- A repair is a schema-checked change to one versioned transformation file, never generated code or SQL.
- Investigations start from a button rather than automatically, to conserve your Codex allowance (`DTM_AUTO_INVESTIGATE=1` changes that).

## State of your machine
- I started Docker Desktop and a Postgres container.
- The dashboard is running at http://127.0.0.1:8000 as a background process of this session, with INC-0001 waiting for approval.
- This session used nine Codex turns from your Plus allowance.

## Needs you
1. Open the dashboard and approve (or reject) INC-0001 to exercise apply and verify with a real patch.
2. Push the branch, or tell me to; the Entire checkpoint links only work once it is on GitHub.
3. Open the two traces in neatlogs and confirm they show nested role and tool spans.

Setup and the safety model are in [README.md](README.md); what was built, tested and still missing against the submission checklist is in [hackathon.md](hackathon.md).
